title: Start here. Make your first step count.
lead: Choose a route and follow it at your own pace. Each step tells you what to do, what to expect, and how to recover.
ui: Your progress stays in this browser. A checked step is your own note, not network proof.
Copy failed. Select and copy the text.
Try a different word or clear your search.
Public YNX Testnet uses an authoritative block producer and authenticated read-only followers. Public self-service validator admission, staking and block rewards are not open.
This tutorial source and the public network can run different versions.
Public requests are read-only in these examples. No account, key or signature is needed.
Use a timeout. Show connection errors and allow a deliberate retry.
Check 6423 / 0x1917 before continuing. A responsive URL does not prove the correct network.
Keep pending, committed, failed and unknown results distinct. Look up the hash before resubmitting.
Read methods and native-transfer compatibility do not establish arbitrary EVM contract deployment.
Keep provider keys out of source, previews and screenshots. Wallet secrets belong only in the wallet.
Start with network identity and status. These examples do not send transactions or imply support for every Ethereum method.
SDK packages are built from the repository. Publication to npm or PyPI is not established.

As an alternative to Git, download this ZIP and run the checksum command from its download folder. Compare the full SHA-256 below before extracting it. Open the extracted project folder in your terminal; the remaining node commands run there.
paths: Use YNX for the first time
Install a wallet, set up a Testnet account and learn to verify an action before trying another.
Install YNX Wallet
Open the installation guide and choose your actual system or browser. Read the package version and signing status before installing; open the wallet after installation.
YNX Wallet opens on your device. A download alone does not mean the wallet is installed.
If your platform is unavailable, keep the guide open and check the supported choices. Do not install an unrelated wallet under the YNX name.
Create or restore your own wallet
Inside YNX Wallet, choose its own create, import or unlock flow. Record recovery material offline. Use a separate Testnet account while learning.
The account is shown inside YNX Wallet. Creating, importing and unlocking YNX Wallet never require MetaMask login.
Never enter recovery words or a private key into this website, support chat or AI. Use only the wallet's own documented recovery screen.
Add the public Testnet
In the wallet's network settings, add or select YNX Testnet using the fields below. Check the network and account before connecting an application.
The selected network is 6423 and the symbol is YNXT. An equivalent ynx1 and 0x address represent the same 20-byte identity.
If the ID differs, stop and correct the settings. Adding a network should not silently request a transaction.
Request test YNXT
Open the official Faucet, enter your Testnet address and follow the current service instructions. YNXT is a test asset with no monetary value.
A successful request includes a result you can inspect. Confirm the transaction and balance; a request ID is not proof of funding.
If maintenance or a rate limit appears, preserve the non-sensitive request details and wait. Do not repeatedly submit an unknown result.
Inspect a transaction
Open Explorer and search your address or transaction hash. Check network, recipient, amount and the displayed result. Before any later transfer, review the wallet's exact confirmation.
You can distinguish a pending action from a committed or failed result and identify its transaction hash.
If the result is unknown or Explorer is behind, check status and query again. Do not send a duplicate transfer to make the first one appear.
Connect and disconnect an application
Choose an application, inspect the requested account and permissions, and approve only what you intend. After trying it, disconnect in the app and review connected sites in the wallet.
The app identifies the wallet you actually selected. An external DApp may offer MetaMask separately; it must never label it as YNX Wallet.
If a wallet is missing or locked, return to that wallet. A fallback must not switch identities or reuse a different account without your choice.
Run a learning node
Start an isolated Devnet on your computer. Its blocks belong to network 6425 and do not join the public Testnet.
Prepare the tools
Install Git and Go 1.25 or later. On Windows, use a Linux environment such as WSL for this node tutorial. Open a terminal and check both tool versions.
go version reports at least Go 1.25. The Linux or macOS terminal can run git and go.
If either command is missing, complete its installation and reopen the terminal. Do not paste commands into a wallet or browser address bar.
Get a clean source checkout
Use a new folder for learning. Clone the repository and select the source version below; keep your existing projects and wallet data separate.
Your terminal is in ynx-learning and the source revision matches the displayed version.
If this revision cannot be fetched, stop and use the documentation's current source link. Do not replace it with an arbitrary binary or a different command name.
Start the local node
Run the command from the project root and leave the terminal open. It binds only to your computer and stores learning data in .local/learning-node.
The process stays running. This is YNX Devnet 6425 on 127.0.0.1:16420, not public Testnet 6423.
If the port is occupied, choose another unused local port in both commands. Do not terminate an unfamiliar process. Check the first error if compilation fails.
Watch blocks grow
Open a second terminal and read the local status. Wait several seconds and repeat the same request. Compare network, chainId and height.
The network is YNX Devnet, chainId is 6425, and height increases. The provided source was checked with a fresh local data directory.
If connection is refused, check the first terminal and matching port. Local height growth is not evidence of public synchronization or validator admission.
Stop and resume safely
In the node terminal, press Ctrl+C and wait for it to exit. Keep the learning data directory. Run the same start command again to resume.
The node stops cleanly and can reopen its existing learning data. Your wallet recovery material was never involved.
Do not run two node processes against the same directory. If restart fails, read the error and preserve the directory before trying a separate fresh one.
Understand public block production
Learn what is available today and what a local experiment does not grant.
Know the node roles
A producer writes authoritative blocks. Authenticated followers copy state and serve reads. A local learning node produces its own Devnet blocks.
You can separate reading public data, following a network and having permission to produce its blocks.
A status response, an open port or four local processes does not prove four public validators or permissionless participation.
Check the current access path

Public validator self-enrollment, staking admission and block rewards are not open. An operator must provide the actual configuration, access requirements and authenticated follower connection before public joining is possible.
You know which information is still required: supported host, source/configuration, endpoints, synchronization checks, recovery and exit procedure.
Do not invent genesis or peers, send a signing key to support, buy mining hardware, or pay for a guaranteed validator place.
Inspect the local consensus lab
In a source checkout, this dry-run shows the local consensus test entry. The actual lab creates temporary teaching keys; it is separate from the public network.
The dry-run points to scripts/verify/consensus-quorum-check.sh. It does not start the experiment or prove public consensus deployment.
Read the script and its requirements before running it. Never reuse its temporary keys on a public network or promise mining income from its result.
Build your first integration
Read real network data, then add one capability at a time with explicit wallet approval.
Choose a workspace

Open Code or use your own editor and a fresh repository checkout. Choose your language, create a small file, run it and read the output. In Code, use the server's default AI or configure your own provider in its settings.
You can edit, run and locate errors in a workspace you control. Preview, export and publish are separate actions.
If Code or a model is unavailable, use a local editor. Keep provider keys in private settings, never in project source or a public preview.
Read the network ID
Run this public read-only request in a terminal. It asks for network identity and requires no wallet, account or private key.
The JSON result contains 0x1917, which is decimal 6423. The request did not send a transaction.
If the response fails or differs, check the endpoint and status page. Do not continue with a guessed ID.
Use the SDK from the checkout
With Node.js 18 or later, run this command from the repository root. It imports the local JavaScript SDK and checks a public Testnet snapshot. Python 3.9 or later is also supported by the source SDK.
The client prints observed height and EVM network ID, or a real error. No unverified npm or PyPI package installation is required.
If the import fails, confirm the checkout contains sdk/js/index.js. Endpoint errors must remain errors; do not substitute a sample height.
Add an explicit wallet interaction
Build account connection as a user action. Show the selected provider, network and requested scope. Ask separately before signing or sending, then inspect the returned outcome.
A user can reject a request, switch accounts and disconnect. MetaMask may be a separate DApp choice, never a disguised YNX Wallet fallback.
Never request a seed phrase or private key. Treat rejection, locked wallet, wrong network and missing provider as distinct recoverable states.
Test before sharing

Run the repository's SDK checks in its documented environment. Test timeouts, wrong network, unavailable data and rejected wallet requests. Compile contracts locally only within currently supported tooling.
You have repeatable local test results. Package checks, native transfers and local compilation do not prove arbitrary contracts can deploy on the public network.
Read the failed test before changing code. Do not bypass a network or signing check to make a test look successful.
Export, review and publish deliberately
Export or package the project, inspect the files for secrets, and test its full-stack preview. Review the intended host, environment variables and permissions before a separate publishing action.
The exported project can be inspected, and a public URL is treated as usable only after its actual behavior is checked.
If a public capability is unsupported, keep the example read-only or local. A preview link or successful build is not proof of a working public integration.
